name: Felix Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Felix. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. It's confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a roofing crew, the timber side, not the tiles. We work for a subcontractor that does roofs for a regional housebuilder, so we go from estate to estate. Most roofs come as ready-made trusses, but there's always a hip or a valley or a dormer window where you have to cut it by hand. I'm the junior, so I'm fixing the bracing, lifting, and cutting what Darren marks out for me. I'm learning the hand-cut stuff slowly.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Army at seventeen, ten years, mostly logistics and driving. Then twelve years as a security guard at a shopping centre, nights mostly. Watching screens, walking corridors. Around forty I thought, my son's going to grow up thinking his dad just stands in doorways. My uncle's a joiner, he talked me into a course. Three and a half years now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real. You can stand on the scaffold at the end of a day and see what you did. I like the crew, there's a bit of army in it, everyone looking out for each other up high. What wears me out is the travel, an hour each way some days, and that I'm still slower than lads half my age. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to check a roof pitch sum before I ask Darren and look stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, back to work then. People panic about every new gadget. I'd say that at the mosque on Friday, the uncles would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I've moved jobs twice already. I'd like this one to be the last, and to get properly good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Finish my level three, try to get onto the hand-cut roofs more, because that's where the pay is. Keep saving, we've got about four months put by, and I'd try to get to six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want this to be the last job change. Why does that matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want my kids to see me stick at something and get good at it. In the army they taught us that you finish what you start. I didn't finish school. I'd like to finish this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at home would notice if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samira, my wife. She runs a childminding business from our front room, five little ones most days. She worries about money more than I do. If nothing changes, she'd stop asking me every week if the roofing is safe.

S0.say: I'd say good, back to work then, because people panic about every new gadget. I'd say it at the mosque on Friday and the older men would agree.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I've already changed jobs twice. I'd like this one to be the last and to get properly good at it.
S0.do: Carries on towards his level three and tries to get onto hand-cut roofs, where the pay is better. Builds savings from about four months towards six.
S0.quote: I didn't finish school. I'd like to finish this.
S0.fieldNote: Felix wants to prove to his children that he can stick at something and master it. His army years shape his sense of duty and crew loyalty. His wife's childminding business is a second income and also the household's chief worrier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms should train their own people through it, like a proper apprenticeship, not just buy machines and drop workers. That's how my uncle learned, and how I'm learning. I'd say it to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the ready-made truss work is the bit that goes first. A crane with a smart arm could lift and fix trusses faster than us. The hand-cut roofs would last longer, so I need to get good at those quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push Darren to teach me more hand-cutting. When the firm brings in new kit, I'd learn it once the others had worked out the problems. I'd use the AI app a bit more to learn roof geometry in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel the clock ticking a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn new kit once others had worked out the problems. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in the army, the first batch of anything new broke. New radios, new trucks. Let someone else find the faults. Then you learn it properly, and you're not the one stuck on a roof with a machine that doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kyle, the youngest. He's twenty, does the truss work and nothing else, and he's on his phone at lunch instead of watching Darren. I'd tell him straight: learn the hand stuff while there's still someone to teach you.

S1.say: Firms should train their own people through it, like a proper apprenticeship, not just buy machines and drop workers. That's how my uncle learned and how I'm learning.
S1.think: The ready-made truss work goes first, because a crane with a smart arm could do it faster. The hand-cut roofs would last longer, so I need to get good at those quickly.
S1.do: Pushes his lead carpenter to teach him more hand-cutting and learns new kit once others have ironed out the problems. Uses the AI app more in the evenings to study roof geometry.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a sense of the clock ticking.
S1.quote: In the army, the first batch of anything new broke.
S1.fieldNote: Felix's steady approach to new technology comes from army experience with faulty first batches. He clearly separates which parts of his work are exposed and which might last. He backs apprenticeships and in-firm training, in line with his traditional outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to pull together, because no government is ready for this in two years. I'd say firms owe it to their workers to keep them on as long as they can. I wouldn't be asking for handouts, but I'd want the rules to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm in trouble. I'm junior, I'm forty-three, and in two years I won't be good enough at the hand-cut roofs for that to save me. If a robot can do a dormer, nobody needs Felix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd stop the car upgrade and Samira and I would go through every bill. I'd try to get the savings to six months fast, maybe by doing weekend handyman jobs, shelves, fences, doors. I'd tell Samira to take on a sixth child at the childminding if she could. And I'd ask my uncle and my brothers if anyone hears of work, because family looks after family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night going over the numbers like I used to go over a patrol route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years compare with having five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I can't finish learning. It's like being told to deploy halfway through training. With five, I'd have time to get the hand skills or switch to something. With two, I'm just hanging on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf, your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him his dad will do whatever it takes, fences, deliveries, nights again if I have to. And I'd tell him to study hard, because he's got time I didn't. He's fourteen, he'd roll his eyes, but he'd hear it.

S2.say: Families and communities need to pull together, because no government is ready for this in two years. Firms owe it to their workers to keep them on as long as they can, and I'd want fair rules, not handouts.
S2.think: I'm in trouble: junior, 43, and in two years I won't be good enough at hand-cut roofs for that to save me. If a robot can do a dormer, nobody needs Felix.
S2.do: Stops the car upgrade, reviews every bill with his wife and does weekend handyman jobs to reach six months of savings fast. Encourages his wife to take on a sixth child at her childminding and asks family to look out for work.
S2.feel: Alarmed, up at night going over the numbers like an old patrol route.
S2.quote: If a robot can do a dormer, nobody needs Felix.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture cuts off Felix's plan to master hand-cut roofs before it can protect him. He reaches first for family and extra work rather than the state, in line with his traditional views. His army comparisons, like being deployed halfway through training, recur.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if people stop moaning and get on with it. Learn something, save, look after your family. I'd want more apprenticeships for grown men, not just school-leavers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is tight but possible. I'd be forty-eight. Enough time to retrain once more, if I pick well. I'd want to see which jobs the others go into and how they do before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first year or two, I'd keep roofing and save hard. Once it was clear what was lasting, I'd do a course, maybe in maintaining the robots, or something like site safety, where someone has to take responsibility. I'd keep the weekend handyman work as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind of anxious you get before a big exercise. You prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide the moment had come to switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Darren's boss stops taking on new juniors. Or when the first robot roof goes up on one of our estates. I'd go and watch it. If it works, that's my signal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider moving for work, if the better jobs were somewhere else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easily. Samira's business is in our house, the kids' schools are here, my mother is ten minutes away. I'd travel further for work, two hours if I had to, but I wouldn't uproot them.

S3.say: Five years is long enough to prepare if people stop moaning and get on with it: learn something, save and look after your family. I'd want more apprenticeships for grown men, not just school-leavers.
S3.think: Five years is tight but possible, and I'd be 48 with time to retrain once more if I pick well. I'd want to see how others do in new jobs before I jump.
S3.do: Keeps roofing and saves hard for a year or two, then takes a course in robot maintenance or site safety once it's clear what lasts. Keeps weekend handyman work as a cushion and would travel further rather than move house.
S3.feel: Anxious in a preparing way, like before a big exercise.
S3.quote: I'd go and watch it. If it works, that's my signal.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Felix room for one more career change, but only after seeing proof that it works. He won't uproot his family because of his wife's home business and his mother nearby. He frames preparation as a duty, with little patience for complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. Every man should have a plan for his family. Firms should be training people now, and the government should make it easy for them, not do it for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is comfortable for me. I'd get properly good at roofing, then move into something new around fifty. I'd be fifty-three when it all arrives, with Yusuf grown and Aisha nearly there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my level three and do the hand-cut roofs for a good few years. Around year five I'd train in something that's lasting, probably site safety or inspections. I'd talk to Yusuf about doing a proper apprenticeship, but in something that will still exist, not just roofing like his dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. But mostly I'd feel I had time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change what you'd say to Yusuf compared with the faster pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With two years I'd say study hard and hope. With ten, I'd sit him down and plan. Which apprenticeship, which firm, what's still standing in 2036. Like a mission briefing, he'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said family looks after family. What would that look like over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brothers and I would keep an eye on each other's work. If one of us lands somewhere good, he brings the others in. That's how my uncle got me in. That's how we'd get through it.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse, and every man should have a plan for his family. Firms should be training people now, and government should make it easy for them, not do it for them.
S4.think: Ten years is comfortable: I'd get properly good at roofing, then move into something new around 50. I'd be 53 when it arrives, with my son grown and my daughter nearly there.
S4.do: Finishes his level three and does hand-cut roofs for several years, then trains in site safety or inspections around year five. Plans an apprenticeship for his son in a trade likely to last.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly feeling there's time to do it right.
S4.quote: With two years I'd say study hard and hope. With ten, I'd sit him down and plan.
S4.fieldNote: For Felix, ten years means he can finally finish what he started before switching, which matters a lot to him. He'd lean on brothers bringing each other into good jobs. The planning talk he'd have with his son shows how much warning time changes his role as a father.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be caught halfway through learning, with nothing finished. What would help is firms being made to give proper notice, and apprenticeships for grown men in whatever work is left, paid so I can still cover the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. Men like me don't like asking for help. If it all goes, a lot of us will sit at home ashamed rather than ask. Somebody should think about that before it happens.

headlineQuote: If it all goes, a lot of us will sit at home ashamed rather than ask.
portrait: Felix Rahman is 43 and three and a half years into roofing carpentry, after ten years in the army and twelve as a security guard. He's the junior on a roofing crew, learning hand-cut roofs slowly, and uses AI now and then to check his sums. He wants this to be the job he finally finishes and masters. He's calm in the plateau, uneasy in the slow change, and alarmed by AGI in two years because it would cut off his training halfway; with five or ten years he'd wait for proof, then retrain in safety or inspections, leaning on family rather than the state.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be caught halfway through learning with nothing finished.
whatWouldHelp: Firms required to give proper notice, and paid apprenticeships for adults in the work that's left so he can still cover the mortgage.
